title: CodeNib: A Multi-View Data System for Serving Repository Context to Coding Agents
event_hint: CodeNib: a multi-view repository-context data system that materializes reusable lexical (BM25/Zoekt), dense (FAISS), and structural (graph) views per commit, incrementally maintains selected-view deltas across edits, and serves ranked search, symbol navigation, and bounded context through one runtime (with stdio MCP + LSP-shaped skill adapters) to coding agents.
problem: Coding agents repeatedly search, navigate, and retain context from evolving repositories, but today's indexes, language servers, and task-local histories are disconnected: they force repeated discovery, do not map outputs back to a common commit and repository-relative source range, and obscure lifecycle costs (per-edit rebuild vs incremental maintenance). Three coupled challenges: C1 heterogeneous views (lexical/dense/structural need different physical layouts but must map to the same commit and source ranges); C2 incremental freshness (an edit changes each view differently, so graph repair, embedding reuse, and rebuild paths must be selected and evaluated separately); C3 agent delivery (serving bounded context through agent tools).
mechanism: CodeNib builds three reusable views per repository commit: lexical (BM25, optional Zoekt), dense (file-level L0 and callable-level L2 embeddings in FAISS), and structural (a reference graph used for dependency/definition/reference/route navigation). Outputs are mapped to repository-relative path/start-line ranges. Selected views are maintained across edits via incremental delta maintenance (graph repair, embedding reuse, rebuild paths chosen per view). One runtime serves search_semantic/search_bm25/search_regex/search_zoekt, structural tools (dependency subgraphs, definitions, references, routes), and get_manifest; missing optional indexes return explicit tool errors rather than silent fallback. Adapters: stdio MCP (instantiates static serving; exposes semantic/BM25/regex/Zoekt search + structural tools) and LSP-shaped skills (accept an injected static or live JSON-RPC provider, sharing the agent-facing location schema while traces record which backend served). AgentRunner separates index-backed SkillRegistry capabilities from ordinary ToolRegistry primitives; AgentRunTrace records ordered events/context state and UsageTracker records provider tokens. Live JSON-RPC is an agent/evaluation path, not an automatic fallback.

evidence.claim: Incremental update speedup (Q1 headline, abstract): when updated outputs match an independent rebuild across 100 snapshots, graph and vector updates are 8.7x and 25.4x faster at the median. (Reported as an abstract/intro headline; the visible Evidence Pack exposes the claim but not the per-snapshot update-vs-rebuild table behind these medians.)
evidence.value: graph update 8.7x faster (median); vector update 25.4x faster (median), conditional on output-match

evidence.claim: Static vs live symbol-navigation latency (Q3, Figure 9): across 1,000 requests over 100 snapshots, 632 (63.2%) normalized path/start-line sets match the live JSON-RPC provider (437/500 definitions = 87.4%; 195/500 references = 39.0%). On the matching subset, static/live p50 = 0.62/2.26 ms, a median paired saving of 1.69 ms and a median live/static ratio of 4.72x. Match rate is the limiting result: definitions 80-99% across languages, references 22-73%.
evidence.value: 63.2% overall match; static p50 0.62 ms vs live 2.26 ms; median live/static 4.72x; def match 87.4%, ref match 39.0%
evidence.baseline: live JSON-RPC language servers (clangd, gopls, basedpyright, rust-analyzer, typescript-language-server)
evidence.condition: 100 snapshots, 1,000 requests (500 def + 500 ref), normalized path/start-line equality on matching subset only

evidence.claim: Dense-index construction scaling (Q2, Figure 8): median construction spans 3.8-56.7s for L0 (file-level) and 19.3-285.0s for L2 (callable-level); within a model L2/L0 build-time ratio is 5.0-6.4x; all ten LOC fits are positive (L0 slopes 0.029-0.644 s/kLOC, L2 0.186-4.282 s/kLOC). Median warm dense-query latency ranges 20-295 ms across five embedders (SR-Small 137M, Qwen3-0.6B, Jina-Code-1.5B, Qwen3-4B, SR-Large 7B).
evidence.value: L0 build 3.8-56.7s; L2 build 19.3-285.0s; L2/L0 5.0-6.4x; dense-query median 20-295 ms
evidence.condition: 500 L0/L2 pairs across 100 snapshots, five embedding models

evidence.claim: ANN fidelity-latency frontier (Q2, Figure 7b-c): HNSW with ef_search=16 reaches 0.977 neighbor Recall@10 and cuts mean FAISS search from 0.910 to 0.0268 ms (33.9x); IVF at 25% probes reaches 0.965 at 0.223 ms (4.1x). Both preserve Flat's patch-target-file Recall@10 (macro mean 0.620). These are component-local: HNSW saves 0.883 ms on FAISS search while the complete dense-query median is 45.1 ms. Extra construction amortizes after ~1,300 searches (IVF) / ~2,300 (HNSW).
evidence.value: HNSW 33.9x FAISS search (0.910->0.0268 ms); IVF 4.1x; both preserve patch-target-file Recall@10 0.620; amortize after 1300/2300 searches

evidence.claim: Retrieval-plan tradeoffs (Q1, Figure 6): mean dense-query time spans 26-295 ms; at k=10 file recall rises 0.705->0.820 across embedding families while symbol recall spans 0.422-0.638. Pointwise reranking moves the high-recall frontier at large online cost: Jina + 4B reranker at k'=50 reaches 0.858 file Recall@10 in 4.29s vs Jina dense 0.812 in 92 ms (4.6pp gain at 46.6x latency); highest symbol recall 0.742 (Qwen3-4B + 8B reranker, k'=100, 14.1s). Graph expansion effect is unresolved: every model-level interval includes zero, so the study establishes neither a general gain nor an embedding-specific routing rule (adds 15-39 ms to median non-reranked latency).
evidence.value: dense-query 26-295 ms; rerank up to 46.6x latency for +4.6pp file Recall@10; graph expansion effect statistically unresolved
evidence.condition: 100 snapshots, five embedders, optional 4B/8B reranker, graph expansion weight tuned on 58-snapshot partition and frozen on 42 disjoint-repo snapshots

evaluation_context: 100 repository snapshots (mix of languages: C/C++, Go, Python, Rust, TS/JS). Views: lexical (BM25, optional Zoekt), dense (FAISS IndexFlatIP / IVFFlat / HNSWFlat; L0 file-level and L2 callable-level; five embedders SR-Small 137M, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, Jina-Code-1.5B, Qwen3-Embedding-4B, SR-Large 7B), structural (reference graph for dependency/definition/reference/route). Live comparators: clangd, gopls, basedpyright, rust-analyzer, typescript-language-server. Retrieval plans: dense-only, dense+reranker (4B/8B), dense+graph-expansion (RRF fusion, weight w_g=0.5 frozen on disjoint 42-snapshot test partition after tuning on 58). Timers exclude checkout, compiler/SCIP execution, graph decoding, index loading. Agents: stdio MCP + LSP-shaped skills; UsageTracker records provider tokens. Models referenced for agent runs include Haiku (hardware/revision unobserved), Gemma (pinned Hub commit/vLLM version), Gemini (Vertex config + access date, no immutable revision).
limitations: The abstract's headline -trajectory-token claim ('selected context policies preserve localization with 50-87% fewer trajectory tokens than paired grep/read across five models') and the incremental-update headline (8.7x/25.4x) are stated in the abstract/intro, but the visible Evidence Pack exposes only the Q1/Q2/Q3 retrieval/index/navigation results; the Q4 agent-trajectory results table (the 50-87% token reduction with its localization-preservation definition, the five models, and the paired grep/read baseline) is not in the visible evidence, so the headline agent-loop efficiency claim is currently a claim, not a verified fact. The static-vs-live comparison is conditional on output match (only 63.2% of requests match; references match as little as 22-33% for some languages), so the 4.72x latency ratio applies only where normalized outputs coincide. ANN speedups are component-local (FAISS search only), not end-to-end (the complete dense-query median is 45.1 ms vs FAISS-save of 0.883 ms). Graph expansion is statistically unresolved (all intervals include zero). Authentication, multi-tenancy, network transport, and MCP as an experimental factor are outside the evaluated stdio implementation. Reranking requires seconds-scale latency. Lifecycle model fits are descriptive, not universal laws.
project_relevance: Directly on-topic for the agent-acceleration card's question of reducing repeated Read/Grep/Glob and of whether a code knowledge graph / repository index lowers end-to-end task cost: CodeNib is a concrete multi-view (lexical+dense+structural) repository-context serving system that exposes search/navigation/context through MCP tools and LSP-shaped skills, with explicit operation-specific validity boundaries (ranked retrieval vs symbol navigation vs bounded context). The measured frontiers (dense-query 26-295 ms, reranking seconds-scale, static navigation 4.72x faster than live JSON-RPC where outputs match) give concrete cost numbers for the retrieval/navigation operators a coding agent uses. The incremental-update speedups (8.7x/25.4x graph/vector) address per-edit lifecycle cost. Verification gap before project use: the Q4 agent-loop token reduction (50-87% fewer trajectory tokens with localization preserved) is the most project-relevant number but is currently only an abstract claim in the visible evidence; the per-model results table is needed to confirm the magnitude and the localization-preservation definition.

evidence_gaps.question: What are the Q4 agent-trajectory results behind the '50-87% fewer trajectory tokens than paired grep/read' headline: per-model token reduction, localization metric, and the five models used?
What are the per-snapshot update-vs-rebuild numbers behind the 8.7x graph and 25.4x vector median update speedups (output-match subset size, per-view update latency vs full rebuild latency)?
